background.definition: Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome is an array of symptoms and signs characterized by an obstruction of venous return through SVC to the heart, either due to an extraluminal compression or an intraluminal thrombus.

list.listitem: Annually, as many as 15,000 people may be affected in the United States.
SVC syndrome develops in 10% of patients with a right-sided intrathoracic malignancy.
Malignancy of the lung or mediastinum is the predominant cause (65%).

The cancers that cause SVC syndrome are listed here, in decreasing order of frequency: non-small-cell lung cancer (50%), small-cell lung cancer (22%), lymphoma (12%), metastatic cancer (9%), and other cancers (7%).
Nonmalignant causes of SVC syndrome (35%) include central venous catheters; pacemakers; and rare infections, like histoplasmosis, tuberculosis, and syphilis.
Obstruction of the SVC leads to decreased venous return and an elevated central venous pressure. This results in edema of the head, neck, and upper extremities, and rarely cerebral edema.
Collateral veins develop to bypass the obstruction and to restore the venous return.

The adequacy of collateral vein formation depends on the level of obstruction, as well as the rapidity of obstruction. This in turn determines the severity of symptoms. Symptoms are severe when the obstruction develops rapidly and below the level of azygos vein.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Presence of central venous catheters or pacemakers

list.listitem: Swelling of the face and distended neck veins (63%) and chest wall veins (53%) are common signs of SVC syndrome. C
Chest CT with contrast is the imaging test of choice. C
Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the chest is useful in patients with contraindications for contrast CT. C
Swelling of the face and arms, dyspnea, and cough are seen in more than 50% of patients with SVC syndrome.
Headaches, hoarseness of voice, stridor, and visual symptoms are seen in less than 10% of patients with SVC syndrome.
Shortness of breath is aggravated by bending forward or lying down. Ask about the duration of symptoms; prior malignancy or intravascular procedures may determine possible etiology of SVC syndrome.
Physical examination usually reveals edema of neck, face, and both upper extremities. Neck and chest wall veins are also usually distended.
Distended neck veins (63%) and distended chest wall veins (53%) are common signs. Facial plethora and stridor are less commonly seen.
Chest x-ray result is usually abnormal (84%) in patients with SVC syndrome; abnormalities include mediastinal widening (64%) and pleural effusion (26%).

Chest CT with contrast is the imaging study of choice. The presence of collateral vessels on CT scan of the chest is highly accurate as a predictor of SVC syndrome, with a sensitivity of 96% and a specificity of 92% (LR+ = 12, LR– = 0.04).
Chest MRA is useful in diagnosis, especially in patients with contraindications to CT contrast (sensitivity = 94%; specificity = 100%; LR+ = 94; LR– = 0.06).
Another imaging option is transesophageal echocardiography.

Suspect SVC syndrome in a patient with facial swelling and distended veins in the neck and chest wall, particularly if they have a history of lung or mediastinal malignancy, presence of central venous catheters, or pacemakers.
Order a chest CT with contrast to confirm the diagnosis. Evaluate for the cause of SVC syndrome (including a tissue diagnosis of malignancy) prior to treatment.

Emergent treatment is indicated only in the presence of neurologic symptoms or respiratory distress. Both radiotherapy and chemotherapy are effective in the treatment of SVC syndrome due to small-cell and non-small-cell lung cancer. Stents into the SVC can rapidly provide relief of symptoms.
Emergent treatment is indicated only in the presence of neurologic symptoms or respiratory distress. C
Both radiotherapy and chemotherapy are used in treatment of SVC syndrome because of non-small-cell or small-cell lung cancer. B
Stents into the SVC may rapidly relieve symptoms.B
Steroids and diuretics are often used in the treatment of SVC syndrome, although there is no evidence to support this practice. Chemotherapy is also effective.

Nonrandomized trials show that stents into the SVC can provide symptom relief in as many as 95% of patients, with a long term patency rate of 92%. The symptoms are relieved within hours rather than the days and weeks over which chemotherapy and radiation therapy exert their effect.

A study reported a series of 156 patients treated for malignant obstruction of the superior vena cava and found 99.3% technical success, although one patient died due to cardiac tamponade during the procedure. Overall patency rates were 95%, 85%, and 80% at 1, 6 and 12 months respectively.

Stenting can be used for relapse or persistence of SVC syndrome both in small-cell lung cancer and in non-small-cell lung cancer. There is a greater potential for benefit from early stenting in patients with non-small-cell lung cancer. A systematic review of 39 observational studies reporting outcomes for 1539 patients found a primary patency rate of 81.5% at one year after stenting, and 72.7% after 24 or more months. A systematic review of 54 studies with 2249 patients found an overall clinical success rate of 92.8% with patency remaining over 90% at one year. The rates of complications and re-interventions were 5.7% and 9.1% respectively.
Surgical interventions to bypass an obstructed SVC are appropriate in instances in which the cause is benign rather than malignant.
Surgical interventions like bypass grafting and reconstruction of the SVC are rarely performed.
The most common complication from SVC stenting is a misplaced stent (3%).
Emergent treatment is indicated only in the presence of neurologic symptoms or respiratory distress.
An evaluation for the specific type of malignancy should be done before initiating treatment in patients with SVC syndrome due to a malignancy.

Both chemotherapy and radiotherapy were effective in the relief of SVC syndrome in small-cell lung cancer and non-small-cell lung cancer: 76.9% and 77.6%, respectively, in small-cell lung cancer and 59% and 63%, respectively, in non-small-cell lung cancer.

Prognosis depends on the underlying cause of SVC syndrome. The median life expectancy among patients with SVC obstruction due to malignancy is approximately 6 months, with a range of 1.5 to 9.5 months. B
The presence of SVC syndrome does not alter the survival in patients with a malignancy. B
Relapse of SVC syndrome occurs in 16.7% of patients with small-cell lung cancer and 18.5% of patients with non-small-cell lung cancer. This usually occurs 1 month to 16 months after treatment.
